frictionVectors.title: European energy leverage
frictionVectors.details: Algeria retains strong control over hydrocarbons and export infrastructure, but European demand and pricing give external buyers influence over fiscal stability and foreign-policy room.

frictionVectors.title: Sahel and Western Sahara security
frictionVectors.details: Instability across the Sahel and tensions involving Morocco increase border-security costs while complicating Algeria's non-alignment and regional mediation posture.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign oil dependence
frictionVectors.details: International firms remain central to offshore production, technology, and investment, leaving Angola vulnerable to external capital cycles despite state participation.

frictionVectors.title: Debt-for-infrastructure constraints
frictionVectors.details: Chinese financing and construction ties support transport and energy projects but can narrow fiscal flexibility and expose strategic assets to creditor leverage.

frictionVectors.title: Northern insurgency spillover
frictionVectors.details: Militant activity spreading from the Sahel threatens northern trade corridors, agricultural production, and state access to border communities.

frictionVectors.title: Nigeria trade dependence
frictionVectors.details: Benin's port and customs strategy is closely tied to relations with Nigeria, whose border policies can rapidly disrupt revenue, fuel flows, and regional commerce.

frictionVectors.title: Diamond concentration risk
frictionVectors.details: Botswana retains substantial negotiating power through its diamond partnership model, but fiscal and employment exposure to global diamond demand remains significant.

frictionVectors.title: External mineral competition
frictionVectors.details: New interest in copper, nickel, and other minerals brings capital and technology while creating pressure to preserve domestic processing and avoid another enclave-export model.

frictionVectors.title: Mining-sector renegotiation
frictionVectors.details: The junta is seeking greater state participation and local value capture from gold, challenging foreign operators but risking reduced investment, production disruptions, and arbitration.

frictionVectors.title: Russian security alignment
frictionVectors.details: Closer security cooperation with Russia offers an alternative to Western partners, yet opaque contracting and battlefield limitations may deepen external dependence without restoring territorial control.

frictionVectors.title: Informal mining and external trading networks
frictionVectors.details: Gold and other mineral flows remain vulnerable to smuggling and politically connected intermediaries, reducing state revenue and local control. Regional trade routes and foreign buyers exert influence despite formal export controls.

frictionVectors.title: Rwanda-Burundi security tensions
frictionVectors.details: Mutual accusations and intermittent border tensions constrain regional cooperation and raise the cost of securing transport and mineral corridors. Burundi's reliance on external financing further narrows its diplomatic room for maneuver.

frictionVectors.title: External competition around maritime infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: European, American, and other external partners are seeking deeper access to Cabo Verde's ports, air links, and maritime-security networks. Praia is leveraging this competition but must avoid excessive dependence on any single sponsor.

frictionVectors.title: Tourism and energy import exposure
frictionVectors.details: The economy remains exposed to foreign tourism demand and imported fuel, limiting effective control over strategic revenue and energy security. Renewable-energy projects improve resilience but still require external finance and technology.

highlights: Oil and timber remain externally exposed

frictionVectors.title: Chad-Cameroon pipeline dependence
frictionVectors.details: Cameroon controls the export corridor for Chad's oil but captures limited value relative to the wider production chain. Pipeline revenues, environmental impacts, and foreign-operator terms remain politically sensitive.

frictionVectors.title: Chinese-backed infrastructure and debt exposure
frictionVectors.details: Chinese financing and construction are important for roads, energy, and logistics, but opaque contracting can constrain fiscal sovereignty. Security instability in the Far North and anglophone regions further complicates infrastructure protection.

highlights: Russian security ties shape mining access
Gold and diamonds remain weakly governed

frictionVectors.title: Security-for-resources dependence
frictionVectors.details: Russian-linked security personnel and political partnerships remain central to regime protection, creating concerns that mineral concessions and commercial access are exchanged for military support. This weakens transparent state control over gold and diamond assets.

frictionVectors.title: Mining corridors and Chinese concessions
frictionVectors.details: Foreign mining interests operate amid limited administrative reach and insecurity, especially outside Bangui. Poor roads and contested control allow armed groups, intermediaries, and external firms to capture value before it reaches public institutions.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign control of oil logistics and finance
frictionVectors.details: Chad depends on external operators, financing, and the Chad-Cameroon export pipeline to monetize its principal resource. Contract terms and revenue management remain central tests of whether oil strengthens the state or entrenches elite and foreign leverage.

frictionVectors.title: Sudan spillover and external security influence
frictionVectors.details: The Sudan conflict drives refugee flows, arms trafficking, and cross-border insecurity, particularly around Darfur and eastern Chad. Regional and Gulf-linked actors have competing interests in the border zone, limiting N'Djamena's ability to control its security environment.

frictionVectors.title: French Control of Mayotte
frictionVectors.details: France retains control of Mayotte, limiting Comoros' territorial claims and shaping migration, maritime-security, and development policy. The dispute remains a persistent sovereignty grievance.

frictionVectors.title: Weak Maritime Resource Enforcement
frictionVectors.details: Limited naval and administrative capacity constrains control over fisheries and the wider exclusive economic zone. Comoros remains reliant on external partners for maritime surveillance and infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: M23 and Rwandan Pressure
frictionVectors.details: Conflict in North Kivu continues to weaken Kinshasa's territorial control and disrupt mineral-producing areas. Regional security competition keeps external actors deeply involved in eastern Congo.

frictionVectors.title: Cobalt and Copper Bargaining Imbalance
frictionVectors.details: Chinese firms and Western critical-mineral initiatives compete for access to copper and cobalt, while governance and processing capacity remain limited. The state is seeking better terms but still captures only a constrained share of downstream value.

frictionVectors.title: Hydrocarbon Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Oil production and foreign operators remain central to state revenue, leaving fiscal sovereignty vulnerable to price swings and contractual dependence. Diversification and domestic value addition remain weak.

frictionVectors.title: Debt-Linked Infrastructure Exposure
frictionVectors.details: Chinese-financed roads, ports, and other projects provide essential connectivity but increase exposure to creditor and contractor leverage. Infrastructure gains have not yet translated into broad-based sovereign control of strategic supply chains.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Control of Cocoa Chain
frictionVectors.details: Côte d'Ivoire has strengthened producer regulation and domestic processing ambitions, but international traders and manufacturers still capture substantial value. Price volatility and climate stress continue to constrain national bargaining power.

frictionVectors.title: Sahel Spillover and Border Security
frictionVectors.details: Militant violence from the Sahel puts pressure on northern communities and requires expanded security cooperation with external partners. This creates a continuing tension between border protection and dependence on foreign intelligence and equipment.

frictionVectors.title: Base Competition and Strategic Rent
frictionVectors.details: Djibouti monetizes its position through US, French, Chinese, Japanese, and other military facilities, but the resulting competition can narrow independent foreign-policy choices. Security revenues remain tied to external powers' strategic priorities.

frictionVectors.title: Doraleh Port and Debt Leverage
frictionVectors.details: Control of port infrastructure and the legacy of disputes involving foreign operators remain central to economic sovereignty. Heavy reliance on externally financed logistics projects exposes Djibouti to creditor, concession, and access pressures.

frictionVectors.title: IMF AND GULF FINANCING
frictionVectors.details: Debt pressures and reliance on IMF, Gulf, and other external capital constrain policy autonomy. Asset sales and investment deals can transfer influence over strategic sectors.

frictionVectors.title: NILE WATER COMPETITION
frictionVectors.details: The GERD dispute with Ethiopia remains a core national-security concern, with Egypt seeking binding operating guarantees while regional diplomacy remains unresolved.

frictionVectors.title: DECLINING OIL OUTPUT
frictionVectors.details: Maturing fields and falling production weaken fiscal autonomy and increase dependence on foreign operators, gas projects, and external technical capital.

frictionVectors.title: GAS INFRASTRUCTURE CONTROL
frictionVectors.details: LNG and regional gas-processing ambitions require foreign investment and shipping access, leaving key infrastructure exposed to commercial and geopolitical bargaining.

highlights: Red Sea position raises strategic value

frictionVectors.title: RED SEA POWER COMPETITION
frictionVectors.details: Eritrea's coastline attracts competing interest from Gulf states, Turkey, Egypt, and other external actors. Security partnerships can expand state leverage while increasing exposure to regional rivalry.

frictionVectors.title: MINING CONTRACT DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: Gold and base-metal projects rely heavily on foreign capital and expertise, creating recurring concerns over revenue transparency, labor conditions, and long-term resource control.

frictionVectors.title: SOUTH AFRICAN ECONOMIC GRAVITY
frictionVectors.details: Trade, transport, finance, and energy links with South Africa provide essential access but leave Eswatini vulnerable to external policy and infrastructure conditions.

frictionVectors.title: TAIWAN-CHINA DIPLOMATIC PRESSURE
frictionVectors.details: Eswatini's recognition of Taiwan brings diplomatic and development support but limits potential access to Chinese infrastructure finance and commercial networks.

highlights: Port access is the strategic fault line

frictionVectors.title: RED SEA ACCESS
frictionVectors.details: Ethiopia's landlocked status makes port access and maritime infrastructure central to sovereignty. Competition involving Somalia, Somaliland, Egypt, the Gulf states, and Turkey increases escalation risk.

frictionVectors.title: DEBT AND INFRASTRUCTURE FINANCE
frictionVectors.details: Debt restructuring and reliance on Chinese, Gulf, Turkish, and multilateral capital constrain autonomy over major transport and energy projects, despite stronger domestic control of the GERD.

highlights: Transition government tightens control over oil and mining
France and Gulf investors retain strategic access

frictionVectors.title: Resource-contract renegotiation
frictionVectors.details: Authorities are seeking greater state participation and local processing in manganese, iron ore, and hydrocarbons. This may unsettle established French, Chinese, and other foreign operators.

frictionVectors.title: Port and rail dependence
frictionVectors.details: Export corridors and processing capacity remain dependent on foreign capital and technical expertise, limiting immediate sovereign leverage over mineral logistics.

highlights: Tourism and fisheries remain externally exposed
Senegal relationship anchors security and trade

frictionVectors.title: Fisheries sovereignty
frictionVectors.details: Foreign fishing activity and limited monitoring capacity continue to pressure coastal resources and local livelihoods. Enforcement cooperation with Senegal is important but politically sensitive.

frictionVectors.title: Energy and infrastructure dependence
frictionVectors.details: The country relies heavily on imported fuel, donor-backed infrastructure, and external financing, constraining independent control over strategic utilities.

highlights: Gold and oil remain strategic but leak value abroad

frictionVectors.title: Gold-sector formalization
frictionVectors.details: Illegal and informal mining continues to damage land and water while moving value outside formal state channels. Government efforts to increase local refining and enforcement face entrenched commercial interests.

frictionVectors.title: External financing leverage
frictionVectors.details: Debt restructuring and dependence on international financial support constrain industrial policy and public control over energy and infrastructure decisions.

frictionVectors.title: Simandou foreign consortium control
frictionVectors.details: The Simandou iron-ore project offers major fiscal gains but remains dependent on Chinese-backed consortia, external finance, and complex rail and port infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: Bauxite concentration
frictionVectors.details: Guinea remains heavily reliant on foreign-led bauxite extraction with limited domestic processing. Contract renegotiations and export restrictions could raise tensions with investors and neighboring transit states.

highlights: Cashew exports dominate a fragile economy
Political instability weakens resource bargaining power

frictionVectors.title: Cashew value-chain dependence
frictionVectors.details: Foreign traders and processors capture much of the value from the cashew sector, while weak regulation leaves producers exposed to price and logistics shocks.

frictionVectors.title: Narco-trafficking and maritime vulnerability
frictionVectors.details: Limited state capacity and porous maritime networks create openings for transnational trafficking and external security influence. This undermines sovereign control over ports, coastlines, and customs revenue.

frictionVectors.title: Port and Corridor Competition
frictionVectors.details: Mombasa and the Lamu corridor remain focal points for Chinese, Gulf, Indian, and Western commercial influence. Kenya is seeking diversification, but foreign-financed infrastructure still creates long-term strategic and repayment exposure.

frictionVectors.title: Sovereign Debt Constraints
frictionVectors.details: IMF-linked fiscal reforms and pressure from external creditors narrow Nairobi's room to control infrastructure and natural-resource policy. Public resistance to taxation and austerity complicates the government's ability to restore fiscal autonomy.

frictionVectors.title: South African Water Leverage
frictionVectors.details: The Lesotho Highlands Water Project provides vital revenue but deepens dependence on South Africa for financing, market access, and infrastructure. Delays and cost overruns risk reducing Lesotho's bargaining power over its most strategic export.

frictionVectors.title: Industrial Employment Vulnerability
frictionVectors.details: The textile and apparel sector remains exposed to foreign buyers, imported inputs, and shifting trade preferences. Limited domestic value addition leaves employment and export earnings vulnerable to decisions made outside Lesotho.

frictionVectors.title: Iron Ore Corridor Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Iron ore exports remain tied to foreign operators, overseas demand, and access to rail and port infrastructure. Liberia's efforts to secure greater local revenue and processing must contend with powerful concession and logistics interests.

frictionVectors.title: Mining Governance and Community Consent
frictionVectors.details: Gold, iron ore, and emerging critical-mineral prospects attract competing foreign investors while communities demand stronger compensation and environmental safeguards. Weak state capacity can convert concession disputes into broader legitimacy challenges.

frictionVectors.title: Competing Control of Oil Infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: Rival political and armed networks continue to treat fields, terminals, and export decisions as sources of political leverage. Production remains vulnerable to blockades, leadership disputes, and contested authority around the National Oil Corporation.

frictionVectors.title: External Military Competition
frictionVectors.details: Foreign security partnerships, advisers, and mercenary-linked networks continue to shape Libya's internal balance. This limits unified sovereign control over borders, bases, and energy infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Control of Mining Value Chains
frictionVectors.details: Nickel, cobalt, ilmenite, and other mineral projects remain dominated by foreign capital, technology, and export logistics. Madagascar captures revenue and employment but retains limited control over pricing, processing, and downstream value.

frictionVectors.title: Port and Energy Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Mining operations depend on dedicated ports, imported energy, and external infrastructure providers, creating leverage for investors and lenders. Weak domestic transport networks also constrain the state's ability to integrate resource regions into the national economy.

highlights: Energy and fertilizer dependence remain acute

frictionVectors.title: IMF-Led Fiscal Consolidation
frictionVectors.details: Debt restructuring and donor conditionality strongly shape Malawi's fiscal and development choices. External financing remains essential for stabilizing reserves and funding basic services.

frictionVectors.title: Power and Input Import Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Hydropower vulnerability, fuel imports, and reliance on imported fertilizer expose the economy to external price shocks. Efforts to diversify generation and agricultural inputs remain underfunded.

frictionVectors.title: Russian Security Partnership
frictionVectors.details: Bamako has reduced reliance on France and expanded security cooperation with Russian-linked forces, increasing autonomy from Western partners while creating new political and operational dependencies.

frictionVectors.title: Mining Control and Sanctions Exposure
frictionVectors.details: The government is seeking a larger share of gold revenues and tighter control over foreign miners. Disputes with international companies and regional sanctions continue to threaten investment and export stability.

frictionVectors.title: Offshore Gas Partnership Dependence
frictionVectors.details: The Greater Tortue Ahmeyim project offers new revenue and diplomatic leverage, but foreign operators and export infrastructure retain substantial control over monetization and technical capacity.

frictionVectors.title: Mineral and Rail Infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: Iron-ore exports depend heavily on foreign capital, rail logistics, and global commodity demand. Expanding downstream processing is constrained by limited domestic power and industrial capacity.

frictionVectors.title: Chagos Base Negotiations
frictionVectors.details: Mauritius has strengthened its sovereignty claim over the Chagos Archipelago, but implementation of any settlement remains tied to British and American security interests around Diego Garcia.

frictionVectors.title: External Energy and Food Exposure
frictionVectors.details: The island remains reliant on imported fuel and food, leaving it vulnerable to shipping disruptions and price volatility. Renewable expansion and regional trade provide partial mitigation.

highlights: Western Sahara remains core sovereignty test

frictionVectors.title: Western Sahara Recognition Contest
frictionVectors.details: Morocco continues converting diplomatic support for its autonomy plan into investment and infrastructure commitments. Algeria and the Polisario Front remain the principal counterweights, sustaining regional tension.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Capital in Critical Infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: Chinese, European, Gulf, and American partners support ports, renewables, automotive, and green-hydrogen projects. Rabat retains considerable leverage, but financing and technology dependencies remain significant.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Security and LNG Access
frictionVectors.details: The LNG sector remains dependent on external energy companies and foreign-backed security assistance. Insurgent activity in Cabo Delgado continues to constrain Maputo's effective control over strategic gas assets.

frictionVectors.title: Port and Corridor Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Mozambique's transport corridors and ports attract competing regional and international interests. Weak state capacity leaves infrastructure governance vulnerable to commercial and geopolitical bargaining.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Capital in Offshore Energy
frictionVectors.details: Offshore oil discoveries and green-hydrogen plans are drawing major foreign investors before Namibia has fully established its regulatory and local-content framework. Windfalls could strengthen sovereignty, but excessive concessions could limit domestic value capture.

frictionVectors.title: Strategic Infrastructure Financing
frictionVectors.details: Export terminals, renewable-energy zones, and transmission networks require substantial external financing. Competition among European, Chinese, and regional partners gives Windhoek leverage but also creates long-term dependency risks.

frictionVectors.title: Pipeline and Border Leverage
frictionVectors.details: Niger's oil-export infrastructure remains vulnerable to political disputes and insecurity along routes toward coastal markets. Dependence on neighboring transit states limits the junta's ability to convert resource control into reliable revenue.

frictionVectors.title: Russian Security Partnership
frictionVectors.details: Closer security ties with Russia support the government's break from Western influence but may introduce opaque commercial and security arrangements. International isolation and sanctions continue to restrict financing and technical capacity.

frictionVectors.title: Pipeline Theft and Militant Disruption
frictionVectors.details: Crude theft, vandalism, and insecurity in the Niger Delta continue to reduce state capture of petroleum revenues. Foreign operators remain important to production, while communities demand greater control and compensation.

frictionVectors.title: Refinery and Grid Sovereignty
frictionVectors.details: Domestic refining investment could reduce dependence on imported fuel, but unreliable power and logistics remain major constraints. Financing, technology, and contracting ties with external firms continue to shape the sector's strategic direction.

highlights: Mineral Hub with Tight State Control

frictionVectors.title: Eastern Congo Mineral Flows
frictionVectors.details: Rwanda's strategic and security involvement in eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo exposes it to allegations that conflict-linked mineral flows benefit regional trading networks. International scrutiny threatens diplomatic and commercial relationships.

frictionVectors.title: External Aid and Security Partnerships
frictionVectors.details: Rwanda retains strong state control but relies on foreign aid, investment, and security partnerships to sustain its development model. Pressure from Western donors and regional actors could narrow Kigali's room for maneuver.

frictionVectors.title: OFFSHORE EXPLORATION UNCERTAINTY
frictionVectors.details: Prospective offshore blocks attract external energy firms, but limited discoveries and weak state capacity constrain São Tomé and Príncipe's bargaining power. The government faces pressure to preserve transparent licensing and avoid premature dependence on oil expectations.

frictionVectors.title: GULF OF GUINEA SECURITY
frictionVectors.details: The country's strategic maritime position draws attention from Portugal, Nigeria, the United States, and other partners. Security assistance improves monitoring capacity but also increases external dependence over territorial waters and port infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: HYDROCARBON CONTRACTS AND LOCAL CONTROL
frictionVectors.details: New offshore oil and gas production offers Senegal greater fiscal room, while the government is reviewing contracts and demanding more domestic value capture. Tensions may emerge with international operators if renegotiation is seen as unpredictable.

frictionVectors.title: PORT AND LOGISTICS COMPETITION
frictionVectors.details: Dakar's infrastructure remains central to regional trade, attracting Gulf, European, Chinese, and Turkish involvement. Financing and concession arrangements create recurring concerns over debt exposure, strategic access, and the share of value retained locally.

frictionVectors.title: FOREIGN FISHING AND MARITIME SURVEILLANCE
frictionVectors.details: Seychelles depends on external partners and vessels to police a vast maritime zone and protect fisheries. Foreign fishing access, illegal activity, and surveillance cooperation can generate friction over control of marine resources.

frictionVectors.title: PORT AND DEBT DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: The islands balance Indian, Chinese, European, and Gulf interest in ports, tourism, and maritime infrastructure. Limited fiscal and geographic capacity makes major projects strategically useful but potentially constraining for independent policy.

frictionVectors.title: IRON ORE AND RUTILE DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: Mining remains a major source of export earnings, but foreign operators and volatile commodity prices limit domestic control over value chains. The government faces pressure to improve taxation, local processing, labor conditions, and environmental oversight.

frictionVectors.title: POWER AND TRANSPORT BOTTLENECKS
frictionVectors.details: Electricity and port connectivity depend heavily on external investment and development finance. These projects improve state capacity but can deepen exposure to foreign contractors, imported fuel, and long-term concession commitments.

frictionVectors.title: PORT ACCESS AND REGIONAL RIVALRY
frictionVectors.details: Turkey, the Gulf states, Ethiopia, and other actors compete for influence around Somali ports, security partnerships, and trade corridors. Concessions and maritime agreements can provide revenue while also exposing divisions between the federal government and regional authorities.

frictionVectors.title: SECURITY-RESOURCE NEXUS
frictionVectors.details: Al-Shabaab, weak administrative reach, and foreign military involvement continue to limit effective control of territory and natural resources. Offshore hydrocarbons and fisheries attract interest, but insecure conditions make licensing, enforcement, and revenue sharing highly contested.

frictionVectors.title: RAIL, PORT AND POWER CONSTRAINTS
frictionVectors.details: Freight-rail failures, port congestion and unreliable electricity weaken state control over mineral exports and raise dependence on private operators and foreign capital.

frictionVectors.title: CRITICAL-MINERALS COMPETITION
frictionVectors.details: The United States, China and European partners are competing for supply-chain access to platinum-group metals, manganese and other strategic minerals, limiting Pretoria's room for maneuver.

frictionVectors.title: SUDAN PIPELINE DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: South Sudan's oil exports depend on infrastructure crossing war-torn Sudan, leaving revenues, production and market access vulnerable to battlefield disruptions and external bargaining.

frictionVectors.title: RESOURCE REVENUE FRAGMENTATION
frictionVectors.details: Weak institutions, elite patronage and armed-group competition reduce public control over oil proceeds and increase reliance on foreign operators and neighboring transit states.

highlights: Red Sea access is strategically contested

frictionVectors.title: GOLD AND WAR FINANCE
frictionVectors.details: Gold production and smuggling remain central to financing rival armed networks, while external buyers and sponsors compete for access outside effective civilian state oversight.

frictionVectors.title: PORT AND RED SEA LEVERAGE
frictionVectors.details: Control of Port Sudan and Red Sea infrastructure carries outsized strategic value, drawing Gulf, Russian and regional interest amid the conflict and weakening unified national control.

highlights: Resource nationalism is becoming more institutionalized
Ports and gas projects attract strategic capital

frictionVectors.title: LNG AND MINING NEGOTIATIONS
frictionVectors.details: Large gas and mineral projects offer major fiscal gains but require Tanzania to balance investor demands, local-content expectations and tighter state oversight.

frictionVectors.title: CORRIDOR DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: Rail, port and pipeline investment by foreign partners is improving connectivity while creating long-term leverage over export routes and strategic infrastructure.

highlights: Lomé remains a regional logistics hub

frictionVectors.title: PORT AND TRADE-HUB INFLUENCE
frictionVectors.details: Foreign-backed investment around the Port of Lomé strengthens revenue potential but also gives external commercial actors influence over a critical national gateway.

frictionVectors.title: PHOSPHATE VALUE-CHAIN LIMITS
frictionVectors.details: Togo retains formal control over phosphate resources, yet financing, technology and downstream-market dependence constrain its ability to capture full value from production.

highlights: State control tightens as fiscal space narrows

frictionVectors.title: EU migration and financing leverage
frictionVectors.details: European cooperation on migration, budget support, and trade gives Brussels significant leverage over Tunisian policy. Disputes over sovereignty and human-rights conditions periodically strain the relationship.

frictionVectors.title: Imported energy vulnerability
frictionVectors.details: Dependence on imported hydrocarbons and constrained domestic investment expose Tunisia to price shocks and external financing pressure. Renewable-energy projects are advancing, but their financing and export orientation raise questions about local control.

highlights: Oil sovereignty advances through state-led development

frictionVectors.title: EACOP financing and environmental conflict
frictionVectors.details: The Uganda-Tanzania oil corridor is central to Kampala's resource strategy but remains contested by environmental groups, Western institutions, and affected communities. Chinese and Gulf-linked commercial interests provide alternatives to Western finance while increasing geopolitical complexity.

frictionVectors.title: Chinese infrastructure dependence
frictionVectors.details: Chinese contractors and lenders remain important to transport, energy, and industrial infrastructure. Debt-service obligations and project terms can constrain Uganda's bargaining room even as they accelerate connectivity.

highlights: Debt and power constraints remain binding

frictionVectors.title: Critical-minerals competition
frictionVectors.details: Zambia is using competition among Chinese, Western, and regional investors to seek greater local processing and fiscal returns from copper and cobalt. Persistent dependence on foreign capital and technology limits how quickly this leverage translates into sovereign control.

frictionVectors.title: Electricity and transport bottlenecks
frictionVectors.details: Hydropower shortages and vulnerable regional transport corridors threaten mining output and broader industrialization. Reliance on imported power and external infrastructure finance creates exposure to neighboring states and creditors.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign control of mineral value chains
frictionVectors.details: Chinese and other foreign firms remain prominent in lithium, platinum, and gold operations, while Zimbabwe struggles to secure substantial domestic refining and processing. Export restrictions signal greater state ambition but have not resolved financing, technology, and governance gaps.

frictionVectors.title: Sanctions and payment-system isolation
frictionVectors.details: Western sanctions, restricted access to concessional finance, and chronic currency instability increase reliance on non-Western lenders and commodity-backed arrangements. This narrows policy space and weakens the state's ability to negotiate from strength.
